blocks.heading: Amalek's brazenness and the second day

paragraphs.text: The Rav begins with Amalek's trait of brazenness. When all the nations trembled at the Jews, Amalek alone felt no fear, and so on Purim the descendants of Amalek rose against the Jews and thereby revealed who they were. On the first day five hundred were killed in Shushan; yet on the second day three hundred more appeared.
He asks where these new Amalekites came from, and why Esther, requesting a second day, asked only then that Haman's ten sons be hanged and not on the first day.

blocks.heading: Purim for the low, Shushan Purim for the high

paragraphs.text: To answer, the Rav distinguishes the two days. Purim is for the lowest levels, where the light of Mordechai lowers itself to strengthen Jews; Shushan Purim is for the higher ones, the walled cities tied to Jerusalem. He brings the Targum Sheni that Mordechai, 'who was exiled from Jerusalem' of his own accord, really lived in Jerusalem and went to Shushan only to raise Esther.

Why not bring her to Jerusalem? Because the light of Mordechai is revealed only within Esther, hester panim, and Mordechai wished to plant for all generations that hidden Jews could bind themselves to it. So he raised Esther in exile, as the passuk says he 'was raising Hadassah, she is Esther'.

blocks.heading: Each by his level, and finer Amalekites

paragraphs.text: The Rav explains that every Jew is judged by his level: what is permitted for one is a sin for a higher Jew. So too there are levels of Amalek. The three hundred of the second day carried a finer spark of Amalek; to a simple Jew they are not Amalek at all, but to the Shushan Purim Jew they are, and so they sprang up only then.

He adds that physical Amalek corresponds to the evil inclination: one who is not drawn by a given Amalek need not kill it. Shushan is in truth Jerusalem, and the Mishnah names the Temple Mount's eastern gate the Shushan gate.
In Shushan the light is no longer called Esther but Shoshanah. Esther is hiddenness; Shoshanah is the rose that blooms in open beauty, as in 'like a rose among thorns'.

Therefore, the Rav says, both days must be kept: Jews outside rejoice with the talmid chacham bound to Mordechai, and the Jews of Jerusalem rejoice with those in exile, for 'they accepted upon themselves and all who joined them'.

blocks.heading: Haman, his ten sons, and inner Torah

paragraphs.text: Haman, the Rav explains, is the root of all impurity, set against the basic emunah that nothing in the world is chance and that Hashem watches over everything. That threat touches every Jew, so Haman himself was hanged on Purim. His ten sons are the ten powers of the soul, and only of the Shushan Purim Jew is it expected that he uproot every trace of them; hence Esther asked for them on the second day.

He notes that where the inner Torah took hold, among the Ba'al Shem Tov's disciples, Shushan Purim became a full Yom Tov, greater even than Rosh Chodesh; elsewhere it has not yet taken root. When Moshiach comes and all Jews are 'walled', Shushan Purim will be kept throughout the world.

blocks.heading: The Targum on Mordechai's refusal to bow

paragraphs.text: The Rav reads the passuk that all the king's servants bowed to Haman while Mordechai would not, together with the Targum Sheni. There were two things: an idol Haman had set up, and Haman himself. Mordechai bowed to neither: not to the idol because he was a Jew, and not to Haman because Haman had sold himself to him as a slave for a loaf of bread.

Then, on the night the king could not sleep, the Jews gathered and complained that Mordechai's refusal had brought the decree. He answered that Haman wore images on his garment front and back, so bowing to him was bowing to an idol, and they fell silent. The Rav points out that this contradicts the Targum's earlier account, where Haman himself was no idol.
He raises a second question: the Targum says Mordechai's Sanhedrin sat at the king's gate. Why there, in the palace that also held a house of idols, where Chazal say Esther's holy spirit left her?

The Rav brings the Divrei Yoel on the Gemara that Avraham's tractate Avodah Zarah had four hundred chapters, while ours has five. Idolatry has many levels: what is not idolatry for a simple person is idolatry for a greater one, even serving Hashem for others' approval. Avraham, the great seeker of his Creator, had four hundred chapters by his level, and we have five by ours.
He stresses that the Targum, by Rabbi Yonasan ben Uziel, cannot be answered as two differing midrashim; both accounts are true.

blocks.heading: The king's funds and Mordechai's emunah

paragraphs.text: First the Rav explains the Sanhedrin. Achashverosh wanted to be seen as everyone's king, so he supported religions and colleges with grants. A great college like Mordechai's Sanhedrin received the king's programs, and whatever the king funded sat at the king's gate. Haman, second to the king, administered all the funds, so everyone had to come to him.

That is why all bowed to Haman, yet Mordechai did not. He stood firm in emunah that wealth and honor come from Hashem and that it is in His hand to make great. Hashem may arrange that the funds pass through Achashverosh, but Haman can neither give them nor withhold them.
The Jews then complained: since the Targum, and the Gemara too, say Haman was no idol, what difference did his being Mordechai's slave make?

Mordechai's answer about images front and back, the Rav says, was a piece of Divrei Yoel. To believe one must bow to a man because he provides one's livelihood and programs is, at a higher level, idolatry: it forgets that Hashem alone rules and that no one can do good or harm except by His will. Even when Haman is absent, a passing thought that he is the source is the image 'from behind'.

He could not tell the king's servants this; they would think even saying 'thank you' is idolatry. So he hinted: Haman does not give me bread, I give Haman bread. All blessing comes first to Israel, as the Zohar says, and only from them to the nations.

blocks.heading: Knowing the truth, and the dance

paragraphs.text: The Jews fell silent because they understood. The Rav says that whether or not one holds at this level, every Jew must know the truth. In hard moments, when tempted to flatter whoever seems to give his livelihood, one must at least remember that everything comes from Hashem.

He compares it to dancing at a simcha: a six-foot man jumps to six and a half feet, then falls back. In elevated times a Jew leaps above himself to Mordechai's level, knowing that Hashem alone makes great and gives livelihood.

The Rav notes that the Rema treats Shushan Purim as a day of joy and asks what it means to Jews not in Jerusalem. Every Jew is Jerusalem, as the Zohar teaches; every Jewish heart is a Mikdash. A person may feel he wasted Purim; let him remember that Jerusalem received Shushan Purim for its honor, and that it now lies in ruins.

Yet no Jew thinks Jerusalem is lost; Hashem will rebuild it, and what happens to Jerusalem will happen to every Jew. So no Jew should despair. The Rav closes with 'the Jews had light and joy', and Hashem's tefillin proclaiming Israel one nation; Hashem glories in every Jew.

The Rav brings the Gemara: Esther asked the Sages to write her for generations, and they answered that Amalek is written three times and not four, in Beshalach, in Zachor, and in Shmuel at Shaul's war with Agag. Tannaim and Shmuel dispute whether Esther defiles the hands, though the Megillah has laws of holy writing.

He explains that the twenty-four books, as Rashi brings, are the twenty-four ornaments of a bride, the Shechinah. Each prophet brought down an ornament already prepared in heaven, as the Midrash says every prophet received his prophecy at Sinai.

blocks.heading: The light of Moshiach in the Megillah

paragraphs.text: The Likkutei Torah of Chernobyl says the Megillah holds the light of Moshiach. That light will be too great to bear, so Hashem gave us the Megillah and Purim to grow used to it. Hence, as the Rambam rules, the Megillah remains when others are annulled: Purim's essence is the wiping out of Amalek, the preparation for Moshiach.
Until that is complete, the Megillah's holiness is not yet in its full expression.

blocks.heading: The seudah of Shushan Purim as a bris

paragraphs.text: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar: the Megillah needs the laws of holy writings as an object of mitzvah on Purim, like a lulav on Sukkos, but not after Purim. The light comes down on Purim, but full holiness awaits the wiping out of Amalek.

A bris milah also gives a glimmer of Moshiach: the orlah is removed and the holy point revealed. So, he says, citing the Chasam Sofer, the seudah of Shushan Purim is a seudas bris milah. In the Megillah Jerusalem is written with a yud, the revealed point.

blocks.heading: Blessing for the bris; why only three times

paragraphs.text: Today, the Rav says, the seudah of Shushan Purim is also a seudas milah, and he blesses the child, from a family of Torah and Chassidus, that as he entered the bris so he enter Torah, chuppah and good deeds.

Returning to 'three and not four', he explains that Yehoshua only weakened Amalek, Shaul left Agag, and in the Megillah Hashem's name is hidden. Amalek was never fully destroyed, so the Sages did not want to write it a fourth time until they found a passuk for it.

blocks.heading: Bells on the hem: Esther's Yom Tov for the last generation

paragraphs.text: The Rav speaks of the Kohen Gadol's robe, which covered him from top to bottom and includes all the generations of Israel down to the lowest. The bells and pomegranates on its hem hint at the end of time, the souls before Moshiach. They are the Jews of whom the Gemara says even the empty ones are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate, and before Hashem they are gold.

Esther wanted Jews bound to Jerusalem but could not ask Achashverosh for a Yom Tov for Jerusalem, as his feast celebrated that the Mikdash was not rebuilt. So she named Shushan, knowing Shushan would leave no trace while Jerusalem remains, the one place that is surely walled.

The day is for Jews outside Jerusalem who bind the end, the generation of Moshiach's footsteps, to the beginning, Jerusalem. He closes with a blessing for wonders as in Mordechai's days and the rebuilding of Jerusalem.
